title: CLO 2026 Academic Month  Research on High-Fidelity Fabric Digital Reconstruction Methods
description: CLO 2026 Official Academic Monthly Course Review Now Available! Associate Professor Zhang Xianglei from Guangdong Polytechnic of Light Industry provides a detailed introduction to the entire digital fabric production process.
transcript:
Hello everyone, today I will share with you some of my teaching and practical experience.  
My topic is the digitalization of high-precision fabrics.  
In our regular work, it often goes like this:  
For example, your client or your own research has a piece of this kind of fabric.  
Then you need to digitize it and apply it to your model,  
so that its light, details, and roughness are relatively well restored.  
And the color must be accurate, including the scale.  
This process requires certain skills and methods.  
So today I will share with you from several aspects.  
Mainly, I will share from three aspects:  
First, the workflow for digitizing fabrics.  
Second, the basic knowledge of our common 3D PBR maps.  
Third, the scanning and processing methods for digitized fabrics.  

The first part is the actual workflow.  
The process is divided into four main parts:  
First, shooting or scanning the fabric.  
Second, fabric production.  
Third, uploading the fabric.  
Fourth, using the fabric.  

So the actual work is divided into these parts:  
First, you scan or shoot your pattern using your method.  
The requirement is that the lighting is as uniform as possible,  
and that the clarity is relatively high.  
Second, carry out reasonable construction,  
because you need to find the repeat unit.  
Many clothing fabrics have a repeating circular pattern,  
so you need to identify it.  
Third, in many cases, you need to restore the color accurately.  
If the color is inaccurate,  
then this process loses much of its meaning.  
Fourth, besides the pattern on the surface,  
you also need to create other maps,  
including glossiness, blur, transparency, etc. These all need processing.  
Fifth, combine your pattern maps with the physical properties,  
then simulate to form a material.  
Finally, store it locally or upload it to a platform,  
to create a cloud disk for storage and sharing.  

In summary, these are the six main steps.  

Second, I will introduce the basic knowledge of PBR maps.  
Our 3D blur and other maps are created and simulated in a PBR manner.  
This mapping includes most of these types:  

There is a visual map, or you can call it a diffuse/albedo map.  
It is the basic color texture of the fabric.  
There is also a normal map, which is a visual effect formed by computer reflection simulation.  
For example, different hairline textures, the degree of depth varies,  
but it is a visual simulation of depth, not actual geometry.  

The third is the height map, which represents the height variations of a few millimeters or centimeters in rendering.  
The fourth is the smoothness map, also called the reflection or roughness map.  
The fifth is the metallic map, representing the metal texture of the surface.  
The last one is the transparency (alpha) map.  

So there are six types of maps in total. Let's look at them one by one:  

The texture map shows the color and surface texture,  
usually a linear mapping of the pattern.  
The normal map simulates the small surface details visually through reflections.  
The displacement or height map shows the real geometry height,  
used to represent actual surface bumps or indentations.  
The roughness map determines reflectivity and smoothness: white means rough (less smooth), black means smooth.  
The metallic map is a black and white image where white represents metal areas and black non-metal areas.  
The alpha map controls transparency: black areas are transparent, white areas are opaque, with grayscale representing partial transparency.  

Our clothing fabrics differ from image printing.  
For example, fabric patterns have surface textures that must clearly represent the fabric category.  
This is the texture used in CLO software.  

The second map is called the normal map or hairline pattern.  
It is a visual effect created by reflection simulation in computer rendering.  
Though it looks like surface detachment, it is actually a shallow visual simulation.  

The third type is a displacement map.  
For CLO, it is mainly a grayscale image where white areas appear raised in rendering,  
and black areas remain unchanged.  
The whiter the area, the thicker or higher it is.  
Sometimes to make the displacement look more natural, it is slightly blurred or softened.  

The fourth one is the metallic map, a black and white image where white indicates metallic areas.  
Adding metallic maps enhances the metallic feel of the fabric in rendering.  

The fifth is the roughness map (sometimes called reflection map), which influences surface smoothness.  
White means rough (matte), black means smooth (glossy).  
If combined with the metallic map, they produce a realistic metal surface effect.  

The last one is the transparency (alpha) map.  
Black areas represent transparency, white areas represent opacity.  
This is often soft at the edges for smooth transitions.  

So these are the six main types of maps used in fabric digitization.  

Next, let's talk about how to obtain the material data.  
Materials can sometimes be downloaded from the internet, but such materials are often different from what you see in reality,  
and the actual needs often differ as well.  
So if you want to digitize real-world fabrics, you need physical methods.  

The first common method is using a flatbed scanner.  
It has advantages and disadvantages.  

The second is shooting with a camera.  
This method is used more often in the clothing industry, involving a camera and a lightbox.  

The third is using a normal camera, which is the most commonly used by users.  

The fourth is using a microscope or magnifier.  
We are not talking about USB microscopes here, but larger ones as well.  

What are the differences between these?  
It depends. For example, if you scan lightweight fabrics by pressing them flat,  
this might flatten the texture and mix the layers, which is undesirable.  
So shooting methods are generally better for such fabrics.  
However, for materials with strong hairiness, shiny parts, or laser effects,  
adjusting the parameters in specialized software can yield better results.  

In other words, there is no one-size-fits-all equipment.  

Now let's discuss some features of flat scanning.  
Generally, the fabric is placed facing down and pressed flat under the scanner.  
The recommended resolution is around 600 dpi; if you want higher quality, 800 dpi is fine.  
300 dpi is too low, so 600 is the common recommendation.  

The preferred image format is PNG because it supports transparency and maintains consistency.  

When scanning, select the area to scan.  
For example, using an Epson scanner, the interface offers professional settings such as color depth (24-bit or 48-bit), size, and naming options.  

There are some technical points to note:  
First, set the resolution between 600 and 800 dpi.  
Second, choose the scan type carefully.  

There are both high-end and low-end scanners costing from hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars.  
The key difference lies in the sensor components, which are similar to camera lenses.  

There are two types of sensor components: CCD and CIS.  
CIS is cheaper and faster but less accurate.  
CCD is more professional, better at color restoration, and has depth of field capabilities.  

Depth of field means that if your fabric is placed inside a frame with a glass surface a few millimeters above,  
a CCD scanner can focus properly through the glass, while CIS scanners require the fabric to be pressed flat.  

CIS scanners have the advantage of faster scanning, so the choice depends on your needs.  

For example, I use the Epson V850, which is a CCD scanner with two lenses.  
One lens is for scanning films, where the film is clipped below and separated from the glass surface by a few millimeters, allowing proper focus.  

If you encounter small fabrics that are difficult to scan with CCD,  
you can buy a magnetic clip to adjust the focus distance so the fabric is not pressed flat,  
which preserves texture.  

Generally, scanners press the fabric flat and are not suitable for more three-dimensional fabrics.  

There are two key problems during scanning: color deviation and sharpness.  
CCD scanners are usually more accurate in color, while CIS scanners may have more color distortion.  

Scanners often produce color shifts, especially for fabrics.  
If possible, use a color calibration card, such as the X-Rite ColorChecker 24-patch chart.  
First scan the color calibration card, then generate an ICC color profile stored on your computer.  
You can then apply this color profile during scanning to improve color accuracy.  

Another important point is that your monitor also affects color perception.  
If your monitor is not calibrated, the colors you see may be inaccurate.  
You can use a colorimeter like the X-Rite i1Display Pro or Datacolor Spyder to calibrate your screen.  
If you don't own one, you can rent or borrow it online.  

Now, some practical tips from my experience:  
My home scanner is a CIS scanner, while my office scanner is CCD.  
If I take a photo with my phone, the difference compared to the scanner image is still quite large.  
However, phone photos are still quite accurate in color reproduction.  

I recommend using an iPhone for photos because its color reproduction is better than many other phones.  
Take photos in the morning with sufficient light but avoid direct sunlight for better results.  

You can then use Photoshop to color match the scanned image and the phone photo:  
Open both images in Photoshop, use the color matching function, select the phone photo as the reference,  
and adjust the scan image's colors accordingly.  
This manual method is effective and often improves color accuracy substantially.  

Next, large-format scanning:  
I found a video where a foreign company uses an A0 large format scanner originally designed for engineering drawings to scan fabric.  
Because fabric is soft, they use transparent tape to fix the fabric at the starting position.  
The scanner pulls the fabric in with transparent clips and glue rollers.  
Sometimes multiple attempts are needed to position the fabric correctly.  

Some large scanners have a copper plate below and a transparent UV layer above, allowing scanning of very large fabrics with resolutions over 1200 dpi, which is clearer than A3 or A4 scanners.  

However, most large and small scanners use CIS technology, so color reproduction is weaker than CCD.  

The third type is a more professional device called a fabric camera scanner.  
I will give three examples.  

First is a German company, X-Tex, which was an early market pioneer with such devices.  
It is a kit combining industrial camera lenses with a lightbox.  
Inside the lightbox, there is top light, bottom light, and side light,  
and the camera is connected to capture images with high accuracy.  

This device can capture very accurate black and white images and color fabric scans.  

It shoots from different angles and records results accurately,  
which is difficult to achieve with AIGC methods or other software alone,  
since fabric colors vary and their fading and color effects are complex.  

The resolution is very high, and the shooting quality is excellent, especially for multi-colored fabrics.  

After shooting, the next step is to find the repeating pattern unit (the "circular find").  

There are software tools with this function, such as the Vizu company's X-Tex software or PixPlant.  

Finding the repeat unit is challenging because many fabrics have clear textures but complex patterns.  

The software uses different algorithms to find the repeat.  
You usually cannot find the repeat with a single image; the software combines data with algorithms.  

If interested, you can visit the official Vizu website or try PixPlant, which is commonly used for this purpose.  

If you use a lightbox shooting method, you do not need to manually find the repeat; you just input the six maps and find the repeat.  

If using scanners or other methods, you might need software to calculate and auto-generate the repeat from a single texture map.  
However, the accuracy may not always meet your requirements, so manual checking and analysis are necessary.  

The auto-repeat function has few parameters and is straightforward but limited.  

For example, Photoshop before 2022 has a 3D filter that can generate normal maps and displacement maps,  
but the colors and results may not be perfect.  
A 2022 or later version is more suitable.  

If you do not have a transparency map, you can manually create one in Photoshop:  
Use the color range tool to select the part you want transparent,  
then create a black and white map where black is transparent and white is opaque.  

You can then use this as an alpha map, but some processing may be needed to clean edges.  

For large or small fabrics, you need to adjust settings to get clean results; otherwise, the final 3D rendering may not look clean, even if the photo quality is good.  

PixPlant can also find repeats and generate reflection maps, which is the best method for making PBR maps.  

Now, about physical properties:  

For example, CLO initially used semi-manual testing equipment to measure fabric stretch and hardness by bending and using scales to measure weight and thickness with a micrometer.  

These measurements are then used to create physical property profiles in the software.  

If you don't have these devices, cloud-based services like CLO FAB provide physical properties generated based on fabric type and composition.  
They automatically match physical properties using big data.  

I do not recommend arbitrarily adjusting parameters because the error can be large, and fine-tuning is difficult.  

So you do not necessarily need to measure everything yourself; using comprehensive default values usually suffices.  

Putting all of this together results in a near-perfect digital fabric.  

I can show you some examples of my previous work:  
I combined the six maps in a loop, applied them to a model,  
and rendered lighting in Blender.  
The texture and authenticity are much higher.  

For transparent maps, the shooting method works very well without causing artifacts or clean issues,  
which is the biggest advantage of the shooting method.  

That’s all for today. Due to time constraints, this concludes my sharing.

chunks.content: ## Overview of High-Fidelity Fabric Digital Reconstruction This section introduces the topic of digitizing high-precision fabrics, focusing on capturing their light properties, details, roughness, and accurate color and scale. It outlines the importance of specific skills and methods necessary to digitize fabrics for realistic 3D modeling and previews the three main focus areas: digitization workflow, PBR maps knowledge, and scanning/processing methods. --- ## Workflow for Digitizing Fabrics This section explains the complete workflow for fabric digitization, breaking it down into six main steps: scanning or shooting, fabric production, uploading, and application. 1. **Capture the Fabric** Use scanning or photography methods to capture the fabric’s pattern with uniform lighting and high clarity. 2. **Pattern Construction** Identify the repeating unit in the fabric pattern (often circular repeats in clothing fabrics) to enable seamless texturing. 3. **Color Restoration** Accurate color reproduction is critical; inaccurate color negates much of the digitization effort. 4. **Additional Maps Creation** Beyond the surface pattern, generate other maps such as glossiness, blur, transparency, and roughness. 5. **Material Simulation** Combine pattern maps with physical properties to simulate realistic fabric materials. 6. **Storage and Sharing** Store the finalized fabric data locally or upload to cloud platforms for sharing and reuse. --- ## Basic Knowledge of PBR Maps in Fabric Digitization This section details the six essential Physically Based Rendering (PBR) texture maps used for fabric digitization, explaining their functions and characteristics. 1. **Diffuse/Albedo (Texture) Map** Represents the basic color texture of the fabric, showing the visible pattern and surface color. 2. **Normal Map** Simulates small surface details and textures visually by altering light reflections, creating an illusion of depth without changing geometry. 3. **Height (Displacement) Map** Represents actual surface height variations in millimeters or centimeters, used to simulate raised or indented areas in rendering. 4. **Roughness (Reflection) Map** Controls surface smoothness and reflectivity; white areas are rough (matte), black areas are smooth (glossy). 5. **Metallic Map** Indicates metal-like properties on the fabric surface; white areas represent metallic regions, black non-metallic. 6. **Transparency (Alpha) Map** Controls transparency levels; black areas are fully transparent, white areas opaque, with grayscale for partial transparency. These maps collectively enable realistic rendering of fabric materials in software such as CLO. --- ## Methods for Capturing Fabric Material Data This section reviews the primary physical methods for obtaining fabric imagery and material data, emphasizing pros, cons, and suitability for different fabric types. ### 1. Flatbed Scanning - **Process:** Fabric is placed face down, pressed flat under the scanner. - **Resolution:** Recommended between 600–800 dpi; 300 dpi is insufficient for high-quality detail. - **Format:** PNG preferred for color accuracy and transparency support. - **Scanner Types:** - **CCD (Charge-Coupled Device):** Higher color accuracy, depth of field, and better for uneven surfaces. - **CIS (Contact Image Sensor):** Faster, cheaper, but less color accurate and requires fabric to be pressed flat. - **Use Cases & Limitations:** Best for flat, stable fabrics. Not ideal for 3D or textured fabrics as pressing flattens texture and layers.

Photography with Camera and Lightbox - Common in clothing industry, using controlled lighting to reduce shadows and reflections. - Preferred for delicate or textured fabrics that would be distorted by pressing. - Morning light is recommended; avoid direct sunlight. - iPhones are suggested for color accuracy in photography. - Photoshop color matching can adjust scanned images to align with photographic color results, improving fidelity. ### 3. Large-Format Scanning - Uses A0-size scanners or engineering drawing scanners for very large fabric pieces. - Fabric is fixed with tape and pulled through the scanner. - Resolution can exceed 1200 dpi for superior detail. - Most large scanners use CIS technology, so color reproduction may be weaker than CCD scanners. ### 5. Professional Fabric Camera Scanners - Example: X-Tex (Germany) combines industrial camera lenses with a lightbox. - Features multiple directional lighting (top, bottom, side) to capture accurate color and texture. - High resolution and precision, especially effective for multi-colored and complex fabrics. - Captures fabric from multiple angles to record color fading and complex effects that software alone cannot replicate. --- ## Finding the Repeating Pattern Unit (Circular Find) This section covers software and approaches used to identify the repeating pattern in fabric textures, a crucial step for seamless texture creation. - Software options include Vizu's X-Tex software and PixPlant. - Algorithms combine image data to detect the repeat; single images may not suffice. - Lightbox shooting methods simplify this step, allowing direct input of six texture maps. - Scanner or photo methods often require software-assisted automatic repeat detection, but manual verification is necessary for accuracy. - Auto-repeat tools have limited adjustable parameters and may not always yield perfect results. - Photoshop (version 2022 and later) offers improved 3D filters for normal and displacement map generation. - Transparency maps can be manually created in Photoshop using the Color Range tool to isolate and convert desired transparent areas into alpha maps, with edge cleanup as needed. - PixPlant effectively generates reflection maps and is considered optimal for PBR map creation. --- ## Measuring and Applying Physical Fabric Properties This section explains the integration of physical fabric properties into digital materials for accurate simulation.

PixPlant effectively generates reflection maps and is considered optimal for PBR map creation. --- ## Measuring and Applying Physical Fabric Properties This section explains the integration of physical fabric properties into digital materials for accurate simulation. - CLO software initially used semi-manual equipment to measure stretch, hardness, weight, and thickness (using micrometers). - These measurements define fabric physical profiles for simulation. - Cloud services like CLO FAB offer physical property data derived from fabric type and composition using big data, reducing the need for manual measurement. - Arbitrary manual parameter adjustments are discouraged due to error risk and difficulty in fine-tuning. - Using default or cloud-based physical profiles generally provides sufficient accuracy for realistic rendering. --- ## Practical Examples and Final Integration This section illustrates the application of learned methods through examples of fabric digitization outcomes. - Combining the six PBR maps in a looped texture applied to 3D models enhances authenticity and texture detail. - Rendering lighting in software like Blender produces realistic fabric visualization. - Shooting methods excel in generating clean transparency maps without artifacts, a significant advantage over scanning. - The overall process results in near-perfect digital fabric materials suitable for high-fidelity rendering and design applications. --- # Summary This comprehensive guide covers the digitization of high-precision fabrics, emphasizing the importance of accurate scanning or photography, understanding and generating six key PBR maps, software tools for pattern repeats, and the integration of physical fabric properties. Equipment choices, calibration methods, and practical tips ensure the creation of realistic, high-quality digital fabric materials for use in software like CLO and Blender.
